questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: You group 20 photos. If you put each photo in its own group, have you necessarily found a useful summary?
questions.correct: No. Twenty separate groups may tell us little about shared patterns.
questions.explanation: Very small groups can fit the data closely without giving a useful summary. This motivates choosing the number of groups carefully.
questions.misconception: Equating a tighter training fit with a more meaningful grouping.
questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
choices: Yes. More groups always make a better summary.
No. Twenty separate groups may tell us little about shared patterns.
Yes. One-photo groups prove there are exactly 20 natural categories.
No. A group is never allowed to contain only one photo.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: A point is close to others in its own group and far from other groups. Does it appear well placed?
questions.correct: Yes. Its own group seems a better geometric match.
questions.explanation: This is the intuition behind a high silhouette score. A good geometric fit is not proof of a real-world category.
questions.misconception: Confusing geometric separation with certain semantic meaning.
questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
choices: No. A good grouping requires it to be far from its own group.
No. Every point must be equally close to all groups.
We can conclude its group is certainly a real-world category.
Yes. Its own group seems a better geometric match.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: A point sits between two overlapping groups. What could a soft assignment say?
questions.correct: The point has some membership probability in each group.
questions.explanation: Soft assignments represent uncertainty about membership instead of immediately choosing a single group.
questions.misconception: Thinking every grouping method must make a fully certain assignment.
questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
choices: The point has some membership probability in each group.
The point must belong to neither group because groups overlap.
Every point must have exactly the same membership probabilities.
The groups must immediately be given known ground-truth labels.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: A fitting method stops because its result is no longer changing much. Does this prove it found the best possible result?
questions.correct: No. A different starting point might lead to a better result.
questions.explanation: Stability is a stopping signal, not a global-optimality proof. Repeated starts can help assess methods such as EM.
questions.misconception: Confusing convergence with guaranteed global success.
questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
choices: Yes. Stopping always proves a global best solution.
No. A different starting point might lead to a better result.
Yes. Any unchanged result must match the real-world categories.
No. A fitting method is never allowed to stop.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: A grouping method starts with each point alone and repeatedly joins the closest groups. What does it build?
questions.correct: A hierarchy of groups, from smaller groups to larger ones.
questions.explanation: Repeated merges form a hierarchy, commonly drawn as a dendrogram. The distance rule affects which merges happen.
questions.misconception: Confusing hierarchical grouping with supervised prediction.
questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
choices: A list of known correct class labels.
A hierarchy of groups, from smaller groups to larger ones.
A rule that never changes the number of groups.
A model that must predict a numeric target.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: A cloud of points is stretched along a diagonal. Which line would usually preserve more of its spread when the points are projected onto it?
questions.correct: A line following the cloud’s long direction.
questions.explanation: Projecting along the long direction preserves more variation. PCA formalizes this idea for centered data.
questions.misconception: Thinking the direction of projection has no effect on retained variation.
questions.activity: Invite a guess before teaching the idea. Ask one student for their reasoning, then use the next explanation or demonstration to revisit the answer. Do not grade prior knowledge.
choices: A line following the cloud’s long direction.
A line across the cloud’s narrow direction.
Any line: the direction never matters.
A line chosen only from the points’ row numbers.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: Why can feature scaling matter before clustering?
questions.correct: A feature with much larger numerical values can dominate the distance calculation.
questions.explanation: Distance-based results depend on the relative scales of features. Choose preprocessing to suit the task rather than applying it blindly.
questions.misconception: Assuming units cannot influence a distance-based model.
questions.activity: Give students a moment to answer, then explain the correct choice in everyday language and address the misconception.
choices: Scaling supplies the missing correct class labels.
A feature with much larger numerical values can dominate the distance calculation.
Scaling guarantees that every group has a real-world meaning.
Distances are always unchanged when just one feature is rescaled.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: In one sentence, explain one reason why a clustering result should be interpreted rather than automatically accepted as the truth.
questions.explanation: Accept one reason: selected features, scaling, number of groups, distance rule, initialization, or whether groups make sense for the task.
questions.misconception: Treating computed groups as guaranteed natural categories.
questions.activity: Accept a short answer in the student’s own words. Use a few responses to identify what needs revisiting; do not grade terminology.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: What does a K-means centroid represent?
questions.correct: The average location of the points assigned to a nonempty cluster.
questions.explanation: A centroid summarizes an assigned group by its mean position. It need not coincide with an observed point.
questions.misconception: Thinking a centroid must be one of the original data points.
questions.activity: Give students a moment to answer, then explain the correct choice in everyday language and address the misconception.
choices: Always the very first point in the file.
The number of labels supplied by a teacher.
A point that must be outside every cluster.
The average location of the points assigned to a nonempty cluster.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: PCA keeps only a few directions from a dataset with many features. What is a possible tradeoff?
questions.correct: A simpler representation, with some information lost.
questions.explanation: Keeping fewer directions can compress the data, but discarded variation may contain information useful for a particular task.
questions.misconception: Thinking dimensionality reduction is always lossless.
questions.activity: Give students a moment to answer, then explain the correct choice in everyday language and address the misconception.
choices: Guaranteed perfect reconstruction using any number of directions.
New correct class labels are automatically created.
Every discarded detail is proved irrelevant to every task.
A simpler representation, with some information lost.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

questions.stem: In a clustering tree, two observations join together early, at a small merge distance. What does that suggest under the chosen method?
questions.correct: The method regards them as relatively similar.
questions.explanation: Early low-distance merging suggests similarity according to the features and linkage rule, not a guaranteed real-world label.
questions.misconception: Reading a method-dependent grouping as an unquestionable fact.
questions.activity: Give students a moment to answer, then explain the correct choice in everyday language and address the misconception.
choices: They have been proved to share a known class label.
They are necessarily the most different observations.
Their row numbers must be consecutive.
The method regards them as relatively similar.
questions.audience: First undergraduate introduction to AI and ML

audience: Bachelor course; first introduction to AI and ML
revision: All 92 questions target introductory undergraduate teaching. History Part 2 was revised on 6 October 2026 to emphasize causal reasoning, cross-era synthesis and transfer rather than definition recall. Stable IDs and event URLs are preserved. Search Part 1 was revised on 12 October 2026 with queue/stack traces, competing objectives, IDS guarantees and cycle-versus-duplicate reasoning; before-topic rules are explicit. Search Part 2 was revised on 12 October 2026 with frontier-score comparisons, reopening, incumbent equality, relaxed-bound reasoning and a lecture-specific synthesis response. CSP Parts 1 and 2 revised on 17 October 2026: partial scopes, pruning traces, propagation fixed points, local versus global consistency, independent split branches, conflict scoring, annealing decisions and solver evidence.
organization: 16 lectures; each original pack split into two parts; classification has Parts 1–4. Original question IDs are stable identifiers, not new lecture numbers.
